title: Your Support Team and the Fear of Making a Mistake During Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece traces performance anxiety to a specific root cause — anticipated judgment from others — and argues that top performers escape the resulting paralysis in two complementary ways: by narrowing focus so tightly on execution that outside judgment becomes irrelevant in the moment, and by deliberately curating a support network that provides feedback without harsh evaluation. The article's distinctive claim is environmental rather than purely psychological: performers need people around them who won't render a verdict of disappointment, because that unconditional support is what frees them to treat mistakes as lessons rather than threats to hide.
points: Performance anxiety is traced to a specific mechanism (anticipated judgment from others), not generalized nervousness, which points to a specific fix.
Escaping the fear requires narrowing focus so completely onto execution that outside evaluation becomes psychologically irrelevant in the moment.
The article's distinctive claim is environmental: curating a support network that gives feedback without harsh judgment is what allows mistakes to become lessons instead of threats.
quotes: Of the many fears that can undermine performance, perhaps none is more common or debilitating than the fear of making a mistake.
While there are many reasons for why this fear is so prevalent, the most common cause is anticipated judgment.

Short of developing the thick skin of apathy, top performers know the only way to escape this paralysis is to become so focused on execution that the judgments of others become irrelevant in the moment.

A performer who knows they have the unconditional support and love of people who care about them (and will never offer a verdict of disappointment about their performance) is free to perform at their best, without any fear of ridicule or embarrassment.
But instead of giving in to the fear of being judged, the best performers accept that missteps are a natural part of the learning process, and they turn to those around them to prove it.
